SAN DIEGO (AP) — The Chicago team that didn't have the pope on its side is heading meekly into the offseason.
Pete Crow-Armstrong and the Chicago Cubs came out to sunny San Diego and wilted like a tourist without enough sunscreen, swept out of the National League Wild Card Series by a San Diego Padres team eager for redemption and perhaps primed for a deep postseason run.
The Cubs lost 4-1 in Game 2 on Wednesday night at Petco Park to exit the postseason. They came in with the highest-scoring offense in the majors and head home having scored only one run on eight hits.
They were ushered out by the Reaper himself, San Diego's All-Star fireballing closer Mason Miller who allowed Nico Hoerner's one-out double — the Cubs' only extra-base hit in the two games — before getting Carson Kelly to ground out to shortstop to end it. The No. 4-seeded Padres move on to face the NL Central champion and top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers in an NL Division Series.
The loss by the fifth-seeded Cubs came several hours after the Chicago White Sox, who received a letter of support from lifelong fan Pope Leo XIV, swept the Houston Astros in Game two of an AL Wild Card Series.
The Cubs beat the Padres 2-1 in a Wild Card Series last fall at Wrigley Field.
Several Cubs players lingered along the dugout rail watching the Padres and their yellow towel-waving fans celebrate on a 69-degree night.
Players hugged inside the quiet clubhouse.
Crow-Armstrong, the frontrunner for NL MVP after becoming the first Cubs player to post a 40-40 season, struggled to find perspective while placing blame on himself.
"None of it feels good," Crow-Armstrong said. "That's it. So I'm just feeling pretty disappointed in myself, but that's for me to work on."
Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman, the Cubs' 1-2 hitters, combined to go 0 for 15 with one walk and eight strikeouts. Crow-Armstrong had the walk in Game 1. Each of them struck out three times in Game 1 while Crow-Armstrong had a walk.
Asked how he'd process his performance, Crow-Armstrong said: "That's not really for me to answer right now. I mean, yeah, you can look at the scoreboard, you can look at the stat sheet, wherever you get your numbers from, and it is clear to see that I didn't contribute. So, that's not for me to feel about right now. I wouldn't process that well if I was."
The Southern California native, who had 45 homers and 41 stolen bases, said the Cubs "showed a lot of heart and a lot of fight through all the challenge. But I mean, I would say to start, like, I show up. I show up when it matters in these games, you know? I think that would help us immediately, but that's all I got right now."
The Cubs dominated the season series 5-1. The teams hadn't seen each other since July 1, when the Cubs handed the Padres their worst loss ever, 23-3 at Wrigley Field as they hit eight home runs.
"The San Diego group, they threw the ball really well," Dansby Swanson said. "They didn't miss spots often, and if they did miss, it was in good locations. It's a really talented staff. They game-planned for us really well and we weren't able to get traction. We gave ourselves a couple of chances here and there, but, we weren't able to capitalize and keep anything going."
Said manager Craig Counsell: "You've just got to go play well and win games. In the end, we're walking away unfulfilled and disappointed."

item.content:encoded:
Dansby Swanson addressed the media at Petco Park ahead of Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series to discuss the Chicago Cubs' mindset following a Game 1 loss.
Watch the video below:
Q. You guys have talked all season long about this team's ability to kind of reset and start anew each new day. Are you seeing that so far today, and how do you think that's going to be able to benefit you guys today?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think we've all -- this whole year we've had opportunities to respond to adversity, and this is obviously no different. We have such a professional group, a group that prides itself on getting better each and every day no matter the circumstance. So business as usual in that regard.
Q. What is it like knowing you guys have Gausman starting tonight, given his experience in big playoff moments like this and just seeing his track record?
DANSBY SWANSON: He's pitched in a lot of big games in his career, in his life. We were thrilled to be able to acquire him at the deadline just knowing that experience and what he brings, the toughness, the pitch ability, and being able to have him on our team to help navigate through moments like this is a big part of why he's here.
He's been so good for us all year in big moments, and I expect nothing different tonight.
Q. From your experience, what's the key in games like today?
DANSBY SWANSON: Really and truly, it's just about being locked in on every pitch, just laying it all out there and understanding that we're at our best when we do what we do best.
At this time of year, it can be challenging because you go so in depth with the other team and trying to navigate what they're going to do, what we're going to do. I think the greatest reminder is, if we do what we do best, then we feel like we're a really good baseball team.
Q. Yesterday Craig went with Pedro at third. Today he goes with Matt Shaw. You saw what Pedro did when you were out. Just what's it like knowing those are the two guys you have behind the main group when something happens with Bregman or happened with you or somebody else?
DANSBY SWANSON: The depth of this group has definitely been a strength, a guy who's able to play multiple positions, able to put together great at-bats off different types of pitchers, and really just the personality piece. Great guys in the clubhouse and the ability to just add to our roster in terms of whether it's hitting left-handed pitching, right-handed pitching, being able to play second base, third base, slide around wherever is needed.
Without them, I doubt that we're in a position that we're in right now. So thankful for those guys, thankful for what they bring every day. Very glad that they're on our team.
Q. We've asked Bregman questions like every day since that day in Cincinnati, and he came back so quickly. Can you just put it into context, like what he's done and kind of what he's playing through and how kind of crazy it is when you take a step back and see what's happened over the past ten days or so?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think, if anyone knows Breggy, some facial fractures weren't going to stop him. He's dedicated to this game. He's dedicated to his craft. He's dedicated to his teammates, trying to find ways each and every day to not only personally get better, but to be able to help guys on the team get better.
It's been so fun being able to be on a team with him, just seeing what he does every day and what he brings to a group. I expect nothing else out of him at this point, doing whatever he can to be able to go out there, take the field. He knows that we're better when he's out there.
Q. Obviously you didn't really get much game action coming back from your injury. Just how have you been feeling with where your swing is at and just your comfort level in the box?
DANSBY SWANSON: Obviously baseball is a game that's meant to be played every day. When you miss a significant amount of time, it presents its own challenges coming back into it. I think kind of somewhat accepting that and going through the rehab process and understanding the position I was going to need to be in in order to get back to be as good as I can be was something that did drive me during that timeout.
It's like unfortunately, but also fortunately, having that time to be able to just kind of reflect and be able to do whatever I can to get back on the field and help this team win baseball games.
That's what I feel is a strength of mine as part of this group, and so thankful to be part of a group that is willing to step up in each and every way and not to overly say that I have to be the one to get things done or whatever. We're a group, we're a team, and we continue to push forward in that way.
Q. What's it been like to see Pete do what he's done this year with the idea that he's still so early in his career and he's got so much more to learn from and use to get better over the years?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think one of the really impressive things about Pete is the thing we've always seen, the physical ability, just the tools that he has, the strength, the defense, the base running. But to be able to really slow the game down this year and understand what he's trying to do at the plate to be able to -- I don't know if we've seen as significant of like a change in like walk rate or swing rate and all those kinds of things as we have with him.
He's just gotten so good at knowing what he's trying to do, how he's trying to execute, and been really stubborn at sticking to that. I think that's one of the big reasons why you've seen his game go into a new level is the ability to like mentally process things much quicker than it was earlier in his career. I think obviously that will only continue to get better.
To be able to do that at such a young age with more or less the different pressures you may have on you and attention on you, he's handled it so gracefully. It's been really, really cool to watch. Obviously having been somewhat in his shoes before and then being on like the older side, the veteran side of things, it's really cool to see him go through that and handle things the way he does.
Q. Obviously you guys have one of the best defenses in baseball, MVP candidate having a crazy, great season, and one of the best offenses. How important is it to take advantage of a season like this when you have the opportunity in the playoffs?
DANSBY SWANSON: I think each year is its own year, right? I think we don't really pay too much attention to those kinds of things. I think this group knows what it's capable of, so it's always reaching for the highest of heights that it can. That's one thing that I do love about this group is the relentless pursuit of really greatness together.
That's something that we've done all year. It's been kind of like a consistent mentality of ours all year. That's why it's so fun to be in positions like this because this is -- you know, being in situations like this is something that can only add to that confidence and to that mentality.
Q. Maybe a dumb question, but you guys from a distance obviously have a phenomenal defense. You've got great defensive players. That's got to be a huge part of it. Do you feel like this team maybe the last couple years compared to other teams you've been on puts an extra emphasis on that at all or goes out of the way to take advantage of the fact that you have the kind of defensive talent you do?
DANSBY SWANSON: It's almost like the last of a dying breed, right? Just like defense, no matter how great we've been offensively and the things we've done on the base pass, defense really is kind of our calling card.
It's interesting because it's not like something I would say that we like go above and beyond to work on it more. Jed and company have put together a great defensive roster obviously because we understand that defense really can change games. When you have Gold Glove-caliber defenders all over the yard, it makes it really tough on teams.
We understand that going out there and doing our part makes it hard for people to score on us. It's really fun to be a part of something like that. Give a lot of credit to the front office for being able to put together a team that is capable of doing more things than just playing defense, but it's wild when you go from really great defenses to not great defenses and like how much it can change things. We've been so consistent at remaining true to ourselves all year.
Q. Yesterday Gausman was saying that you treat this game like any other game except there's all those yellow towels flying around, and it can feel like momentum in these games in the postseason can feel even more real. What's it like managing that side of the game and the postseason?
DANSBY SWANSON: The biggest thing is accepting that it is the same game, right? It's the same rules other than the extra innings if there's not somebody on second base. But it's the same rules.
And being able to embrace that we are prepared and we've just got to go leave it all out there each and every day, each and every pitch, every inning and understanding that things can turn it one swing of the bat, one play in the field, one pitch, and just consistently attacking each and every pitch, whether it's on offense or defense.
Q. The pitching staff has obviously been through a lot this season. Can you just describe what it's been like watching how Counsell, the staff have pieced it together, especially at this point in the season and in a game like this where obviously it's all hands on deck?
DANSBY SWANSON: It's kind of wild when you like kind of ride it out, just the injuries that we've sustained, the things that we've gone through in the pitching department itself. Give a lot of credit to the guys that are here now, obviously Tommy and the rest of the pitching staff for being able to consistently find ways to improve the group and get guys better.
Then you look at just some of the acquisitions and all those kinds of things and really being able to identify traits that are going to play well at this time of year. It's really impressive what Counsell is able to do really putting each guy in a great position to succeed. It sounds simple, but he does it at a really, really high rate. I think it's something that he's really, really good at.
He's done well for the pitching staff, and they've obviously rewarded him in the same way by throwing the ball well. Very thankful for that and the hard work that everyone's done to be able to get to this point. Hopefully we'll go out there and put together a complete performance tonight.

item.content:encoded:
The best time of the baseball year is finally here. The playoffs begin Tuesday, with a quadruple-header of wild-card games on tap. The schedule for each series' first two games is identical.
Let's break down how each team got here, how they can win, X-factors, series predictions and more before the wild-card round begins.
AL: CWS-HOU • BOS-NYY | NL: PHI-ATL • CHC-SD
No. 6 Philadelphia Phillies vs. No. 3 Atlanta Braves
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 2 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Jesús Luzardo (PHI) vs. Chris Sale (ATL)
Game 2, 2 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Cristopher Sánchez (PHI) vs. Tyler Mahle (ATL)
Game 3, TBD*: Aaron Nola (or Zack Wheeler on four days' rest) (PHI) vs. Grant Holmes (ATL)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Phillies: It was a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde type of season for the Phillies, to say the least. For the second time in five seasons, an in-season managerial firing was needed to light a fire under an underperforming veteran roster that appeared to be letting their window close. But the Phillies, like they've done before, found a way to get themselves going on the back of their starting rotation. The Phillies didn't make it easy on themselves in September, going 10-14 down the stretch and needing to win their regular-season finale against the Rays to punch their ticket to the postseason. But now that they're in, this veteran group will look to show that they're better than the past month suggests.
Braves: It was a reassuring year in Atlanta, a much-needed reminder that no, this era of Braves baseball was not over after their disastrous, postseason-less 2025. A change in manager, from the now-retired Brian Snitker to the endearingly pugnacious Walt Weiss, set the tone. As did a major refresh of Atlanta's coaching staff. That turnover, in contrast with the continuity on the roster, proved crucial as Atlanta waltzed to its first division title since 2023.
Big campaigns from metronomic first baseman Matt Olson and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year Drake Baldwin shocked nobody. The same was true for ace Chris Sale, certain to be voted an NL Cy Young finalist. But few would've predicted Michael Harris II leading the team in bWAR with a dynamic, consistent offensive season. Role players such as Mauricio Dubón, Mike Yastrzemski and Dominic Smith all delivered critical production to help offset underwhelming seasons from the likes of Ozzie Albies and Austin Riley.
Ronald Acuña Jr., that wonderfully mercurial burst of baseballing light, might've fit into that last group if not for an otherworldly September in which he clocked seven homers with a .950 OPS. That renaissance continuing into October would be a game-changer for the Braves, whose 2021 title came with Acuña sidelined.
X-factors
Phillies: Trea Turner
The regular season wasn't kind to shortstop Trea Turner, who recorded the worst season of his career. But the thing about the postseason is that it allows players who have not yet written the final story on their season to become heroes. And if the Phillies want to move past Atlanta and reach the NLDS for the fifth straight year, Turner finding his rhythm would be a welcomed sight for the team's offense. Turner has a .733 OPS off Sale in 25 career at-bats and a very respectable .863 OPS off Mahle in 25 career at-bats.
Braves: Tyler Mahle
Chris Sale is going to start Game 1 for Atlanta, and he's probably going to be pretty good. That feels as bankable as anything in our topsy-turvy world. But Mahle, set to throw Game 2, has been one of the game's most reliable starters since he joined the Braves from a zip-less San Francisco team at the deadline. The veteran righty posted a 1.99 ERA with Atlanta, allowing one earned or fewer in seven of his nine starts.
Mahle's most recent start, however, was a relative stinker. He surrendered five runs and struck out just four at home against an undermanned Reds lineup. And the underlying metrics, it should be said, are a bit more skeptical about Mahle's prospects. That's understandable. He doesn't throw that hard or strike out oodles of hitters. He hasn't conjured more swing-and-miss or meaningfully lowered opponents' hard-hit rate as a Brave. And yet, Mahle has found a way to find outs. Whether he can do so against Philly's bats will be huge.
How they win
Phillies: Can any team in baseball go toe-to-toe with Philly's starting rotation? With the quartet of Wheeler, Sánchez, Luzardo and Nola, the Phillies should have the advantage in a three-, five- or seven-game series. So while their offense is more of a wild card (pun intended), this team should be able to count on its starter giving them a chance to win every time out. And if that foursome gets hot, it's not outlandish to believe they could carry Philly on another deep postseason run.
Braves: It has been a restful week for the Braves, who were able to sit back, relax and line up their starting rotation for this wild-card series. The same cannot be said for Philly, which needed every last out to clinch on the regular season's final day. For the Phillies, the sense of exhaustion is real and gives Atlanta a legitimate advantage.
But it all starts with Sale. If he cruises like he's capable of in Game 1, that puts Atlanta in the catbird seat. Only one team in the current playoff format (the 2025 Yankees) came back to win a wild-card series after losing the first game.
Series prediction: Braves in 3
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 3 Houston Astros
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 5 p.m. ET Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): David Sandlin (CWS) vs. Peter Lambert (HOU)
Game 2 5 p.m. ET Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Sean Burke (CWS) vs. Hunter Brown (HOU)
Game 3, TBD*: Davis Martin (CWS) vs. Hayden Wesneski (HOU)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
White Sox: The White Sox have been easily one of the best stories of the 2026 regular season, reaching the postseason for the first time since 2021. Chicago became the first team in MLB history to reach the postseason following three consecutive 100-loss seasons, capturing the third AL wild-card spot. The offense, led by first-time All-Stars Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami, was the driving force behind the Sox's success. Chicago finished the season with a top-five offense in MLB.
The fact that the White Sox didn't win the AL Central might come as a disappointment, considering they were in first place for the majority of the second half. Still, it's undeniable that any result that puts them in the playoffs is a huge victory for the organization and a fan base that has been waiting for competitive baseball.
Astros: For a franchise that has accomplished so much over the past decade, there's something shameful, even humiliating about raising the 2026 AL West banner. That's because these Astros are, by record, the single worst division winner in the sport's long past. Before Sunday, no team with a .500 record or below had ever reached the postseason. But Houston rewrote history thanks to an MVP-caliber season from Yordan Alvarez and a tidal wave of mediocrity from its AL West counterparts. Their inclusion in the October jamboree is more an indictment of the Texas Rangers and the Seattle Mariners than anything else, but the Astros at least ended on a high note with their 9-0 win over the A's on Sunday.
Houston also deserves a morsel of credit for refurbishing its season after a disastrous April. Reaching .500 with the fourth-worst starting staff by ERA — only the Reds, A's and Rockies were worse — is also an accomplishment worth commending, a testament to something. Where would this club be without Peter Lambert, whose 3.87 ERA in 153 2/3 innings offered the only semblance of stability for a roster constantly in flux?
Things got sad enough, discombobulated enough, that in August owner Jim Crane relieved GM Dana Brown of his duties. There's an overwhelming expectation that skipper Joe Espada won't be back next year, either. It's difficult to be optimistic about Houston's very uncertain future. But in the random present of playoff baseball, anything is possible — especially when you employ the best hitter on the planet.
X-factors
White Sox: Munetaka Murakami
Munetaka Murakami is a game-changer, and his presence in the White Sox's lineup is a huge advantage in the postseason. The White Sox's rookie slugger burst onto the scene in 2026, hitting 35 home runs and providing instant impact in his first season after coming over from Japan. But following a midseason hamstring injury, the league seemed to adjust to him; Murakami finished with a slashline of .184/.328/.423 and 11 homers since Aug 1. Still, he has the type of power that can change a series by himself, and with three homers in the final week of the season, he appears to be coming out of his second-half slump. If Murakami has rediscovered his power stroke, it could change this series.
Astros: Isaac Paredes
Yordan Alvarez is currently the best hitter on earth. He cannot, under any circumstances, be allowed to dictate proceedings during this series. Chicago must make somebody else in Houston's mediocre lineup beat them. If there's a base open with Alvarez up, he should just stroll straight to first every time.
That puts a mountain of pressure on Paredes. The stocky third baseman has been hitting right behind Alvarez for most of the season and has, for the most part, showed well. He's a supremely weird hitter, one who rarely hits the ball hard or barrels it up. But Paredes doesn't whiff, doesn't punch out and has a preternatural knack for pulling the ball in the air. Expect him to come up multiple times in big spots with runners on.
How they win
White Sox: The White Sox's offense has carried them all season, and if they hope to advance to the ALDS against their division rival, they'll have to slug their way there. Vargas, Murakami and shortstop Colson Montgomery each finished the season with more than 30 longballs, and the Sox finished fifth in MLB in homers. For a team built to slug, Daikin Park in Houston isn't the worst environment to play in on the road. Chicago's power-packed lineup has shown that if they're hitting the ball out of the ballpark, offensively, they can play with anyone.
Astros: Houston desperately needs offensive contributions from someone besides Alvarez. Maybe it's the aforementioned Paredes or the en fuego Yainer Díaz. Perhaps Jose Altuve, 36 years old and in full decline, has one magical month left in his Hall of Fame career. But with such a tattered pitching staff, the Astros need to score to win. They also need to win the Hunter Brown start; he's far and away their best starter. They need a lot, frankly. And yet, much weirder October things have happened inside that East Texas thunderdome over the past decade.
Series prediction: Astros in 3
No. 5 Boston Red Sox vs. No. 4 New York Yankees
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 8 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Payton Tolle (BOS) vs. Cam Schlittler (NYY)
Game 2, 8 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Sonny Gray (BOS) vs. Max Fried (NYY)
Game 3, TBD*: Ranger Suárez (BOS) vs. Gerrit Cole (NYY)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Red Sox: Odysseus would be proud. What a winding, bizarre and tumultuous road it has been for the Sox. Boston began the year like a snail on Unisom, posting a lackluster 9-17 record through April 24. That precipitated a dramatic, Red Wedding-style culling, in which manager Alex Cora and several other staff members were relieved of their duties. Extended injury list stints for the team's two most important pieces, outfielder Roman Anthony and 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet, made a turnaround feel awfully unlikely. On July 24, the Sox lost a rubber match in Colorado and traveled home 14 games under .500. Their postseason odds wallowed around 10%.
Then, everything changed. It began with a home mop against the Yanks and fully kicked into gear when the Red Sox hit the road for a three-city swing the first week of July. They went 9-0 on that trip before winning six straight at home. That 15-game streak catapulted them back into contention and the good graces of an understandably unplugged fan base. Between July 3 and Aug. 7, the Sox went a ridiculous 32-5, trampolining from 14 games under .500 to 13 games over. Fenway was a zoo. Nothing could go wrong. Boston ballfans beamed once again.
The heater earned Cora's replacement, Chad Tracy, the full-time gig. It also afforded the Sox a relatively comfortable September. It's worth noting, though, that Boston has not played particularly crisply since cooling off from the volcanic run, with a 21-22 record since Aug. 8. Ultimately, their final numbers and standing in the American League are not shocking or unexpected, even though Boston's odyssey was wonky beyond comparison.
Yankees: For all the stress, the drama, the hand-wringing, for all the injuries and under-performance, 2026 was a relatively straightforward season in YankeeLand. A lot, it should be said, went wrong. Reigning AL MVP Aaron Judge has played just seven games since May. Giancarlo Stanton hasn't played since April. Max Fried and Carlos Rodón each missed about two months. Young players such as Anthony Volpe, Jasson Dominguez and Austin Wells regressed offensively. Gerrit Cole, coming back from Tommy John, didn't fully recapture his frontline best.
And yet, here the Yankees are, with 93 wins and in an identical place to where they finished last year. That's thanks to breakout campaigns from homegrown pieces such as Cam Schlittler (the AL Cy Young favorite) and Ben Rice (41 home runs and a .897 OPS). Closer David Bednar has been dynamite. Cody Bellinger has been a rock. Skipper Aaron Boone kept the train on the tracks. Three games at home against the Red Sox await. Beyond that looms an ALDS against a daunting division foe. We've been here before.
The largest difference, of course, is the uncertainty swirling around Judge. The Yankees' captain missed three months due to a rib problem, came back for a week, strained his calf and went back on the shelf. Boone says he's preparing for a wild-card round without Judge. Judge says he plans to play. What sort of magic this reduced version of Judge can conjure is easily the juiciest storyline ahead of this rivalry showdown. That said, this series, like this Yankees season, is probably going to be dictated by the pitchers.
X-factors
Red Sox: Roman Anthony
It has been an odd season for the 22-year-old, who missed last year's wild-card festivities due to injury. In March, Anthony was a late addition to Team USA's WBC roster. He shined on that grand stage, impressing his more established teammates and earning plaudits from a coaching staff of hardball lifers. That only ratcheted up the hype on a player expected to carry a franchise less than a year after he became legally permitted to drink a beer.
So when Anthony started slowly, disappointment bubbled. Then, on May 4, he tore a ligament in his finger; that kept him out of action until Aug. 30. A lot happened in the interim, most of which Anthony spent rehabbing at the team's complex in Florida. Since returning, he has looked promising, tantalizingly close to unleashing the full assortment of his talents upon the league. Now, with Willson Contreras banged up and either unavailable or restricted, the pressure returns to Anthony's young shoulders.
Yankees: Luis García Jr.
García was a curious character for the Yankees to shape their trade deadline around. Instead of acquiring a piece that filled an obvious void (righty stick with defensive value or versatility), GM Brian Cashman opted to add the most dynamic hitter possible. New York landed on García, who was in the midst of an offensive breakout under a new Washington Nationals regime.
For a month, that plan bore fruit, with the Dominican slugger posting an .846 OPS in August. But since then, the wheels have fallen off, with García's chase rate skyrocketing. His September OPS started with a 5. He has homered just twice since Aug. 26. He doesn't have an extra-base hit since Sept. 10. There's a chance, given Boston's bevy of southpaws and New York's DH surplus, that he doesn't start every game. But García will get his chances, and whether he comes up big might swing the series.
How they win
Red Sox: Boston's pitching staff is the only one in baseball that ranks in the top five in both home run rate and walk rate. That's a rare combo. Usually, throwing the ball in the strike zone more often leads to more hard contact. But these Red Sox hurlers, for whatever reason, have threaded that needle perfectly. No team in the league has allowed fewer homers. However, no team has hit more than the Yankees. Boston revitalized its season behind pitching and defense, keeping the scores low and the games close. Doing so here will give them the best chance of authoring an upset.
Yankees: No American League team can compete with New York's starting staff. But the Yankees need more than dominance from Schlittler, Fried and Cole. They need length. The bridge to Bednar is unsteady. So the longer the starters go, the rosier that path looks. Offensively, the Yankees need a big swing or two from their right-handed bats against Boston's left-handed arms. That could come from a banged-up Judge or Stanton. It could come from veteran southpaw-killer Paul Goldschmidt, trade-acquisition Heliot Ramos or rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. If it comes from the beleaguered Anthony Volpe, the tri-state area will lose its collective marbles. But somebody, anybody who stands on the right side of the batter's box has to make an impact.
Series prediction: Yankees in 3
No. 5 Chicago Cubs vs. No. 4 San Diego Padres
(all times ET)
Projected starters
Game 1, 10 p.m. Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): Shota Imanaga (CHC) vs. Michael King (SD)
Game 2, 10 p.m. Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Clay Holmes (CHC) vs. Nick Pivetta (SD)
Game 3, TBD*: Matthew Boyd (CHC) vs. Walker Buehler or Casey Mize or Robbie Ray (SD)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Cubs: It was Pete Crow-Armstrong's world, and the rest of us just lived in it. Chicago's 24-year-old center fielder went fully supersonic this year, cranking 45 homers, swiping 41 bags and delivering a .945 OPS with his typically elite outfield defense. He will win the NL MVP, and it might be unanimous. That performance shaped and guided and defined this Cubs' season, electrifying an offense that led baseball in OPS, K/BB rate and runs per game.
Alex Bregman's arrival via free agency, too, cannot be understated. He struggled mightily for the first few months, with his extended schneid at one point eliciting boos from a frustrated Wrigley crowd. But since July 12, Bregman leads all qualified National League hitters in OPS. His experience, comportment and leadership, by all accounts, have also had a meaningful impact on Crow-Armstrong.
But pitching woes, in both the rotation and the bullpen, kept Chicago from ever seriously threatening the Brewers for the NL Central title. The Cubs started the year on something of a roller coaster, with two 10-game winning streaks and a 10-game losing streak before the calendar flipped to June. They'll enter October on something of an ice floe, with 15 runs scored in their final six contests.
Padres: San Diego has the best record in baseball since July 24. The day before, the Pads lost a rubber match in Atlanta to fall to three games under. 500. That pushed the club four games adrift of a wild-card spot, with the Cardinals, Pirates, Marlins, Nationals and Diamondbacks standing between them and a trip to October. That was the low-water mark for this team.
Since that date, the Padres have gone 41-18. They won five straight in late July, six straight in August and eight straight in September. They've lost thrice since Labor Day. The reason for the resurgence? Check out these numbers.
| Padres offensive ranks before and after July 24 | | |
| | Before | After |
| Runs/game | 4.14 (25th) | 4.95 (3rd) |
| AVG | .230 (28th) | .268 (2nd) |
| OBP | .307 (27th) | .339 (2nd) |
| SLG | .383 (27th) | .425 (2nd) |
| OPS | .689 (26th) | .764 (2nd) |
San Diego's offense went from bottom-five to top-five. Some of that is batted-ball luck and sequencing. A lot of it is Fernando Tatis Jr. turning back into a monster. Jackson Merrill had a similar rebirth. Ty France continued his bounce-back campaign. Xander Bogaerts shifted from unwatchable to capable. Unsung heroes such as Dustin Harris and Luis Rengifo got hot. The starting pitching did just enough. The game's best bullpen never stopped dominating. It's that unit, led by a cadre of flamethrowers in Mason Miller, Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez, that makes these Padres a particularly formidable October opponent.
X-factors
Cubs: Alex Bregman — specifically, his face
One week ago, Bregman was the victim of some very painful misfortune. A check-swing foul ball off the bat of Cubs first baseman Michael Busch struck Bregman in the face while he was standing in the on-deck circle. Blood dripped from below his left eye as he scurried down the dugout steps into the clubhouse. A trip to the hospital revealed multiple facial fractures. The incident kept Bregman out of the lineup until Friday, when he went 0-for-4 with a strikeout as Chicago's DH. He went 4-for-4 with two home runs and a walk in Sunday's season finale.
There's no doubt that Bregman, the textbook definition of a "grinder," will take the field in October. But at what level? He has been so integral to Chicago's lineup for the past few months that even a slightly reduced version of Bregman could unsettle things. Among active players, only his former Astros teammate Jose Altuve has taken more postseason plate appearances.
Padres: Fernando Tatis Jr.
Nothing is more meaningfully different about this year's Padres team compared to the one that went three and see-ya at Wrigley in 2025 than Fernando Tatis Jr.'s stunning offensive reemergence. Things didn't start so swimmingly this year for the swaggering outfielder, who needed 55 games to clock his first longball of this season. But since May 30, Tatis' .914 OPS ranks fourth in the NL, and his 4.9 fWAR ranks second in MLB behind only Crow-Armstrong.
This version of Tatis looks a lot like the one who took the baseball world by storm en route to finishing third in NL MVP in 2021. Will that brilliance show up in a small October sample? It usually has throughout the 27-year-old's career; he holds a 1.114 postseason OPS in 70 plate appearances. Tatis, though, has never advanced past the NLDS. Remember, he was in PED timeout when the Padres stampeded to the NLCS in 2022. Could this month be his path back to full-blown superstardom?
How they win
Cubs: The margins were razor thin when these teams lined up in the wild-card round last year, with a highlight reel of web gems from shortstop Dansby Swanson making the difference. Those games, oddly enough, were incredibly low-scoring, with Chicago snagging two 3-1 wins and San Diego edging out a 3-0 win. It's hard to imagine the Cubs and their underwhelming relief group winning that way again, particularly on the road. To advance, they'll need buckets of runs. With PCA, Bregman, Seiya Suzuki and Co., that's a real possibility.
Padres: The Padres' formula for success has been the same for the past few seasons: Shorten the game. San Diego realistically needs five innings from its starters. Then manager Craig Stammen gets to turn things over to the best relief core in baseball, led by southpaw Adrían Morejon and flamethrower Mason Miller. The Friars' starting pitching has gotten stronger as they've gotten healthy, so if Michael King in Game 1 and likely Nick Pivetta in Game 2 can each give San Diego 15 outs, the Padres have a good chance of making quick work of Chicago.

item.title: [Bleed Cubbie Blue] Cubs 6, Red Sox 2: Alex Bregman is more than ready for the postseason
item.dc:creator: Al Yellon
item.description: Last Sunday, Alex Bregman was hit in the face by a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch in Cincinnati. He suffered facial fractures and missed three games. Bregman came back Friday as the DH and Sunday, just a bit over exactly one week since that accident, he hit two home runs and also singled, doubled and walked. item.content:encoded:
Last Sunday, Alex Bregman was hit in the face by a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch in Cincinnati. He suffered facial fractures and missed three games.
Bregman came back Friday as the DH and Sunday, just a bit over exactly one week since that accident, he hit two home runs and also singled, doubled and walked. His 4-for-4 afternoon led the Cubs to a 4-2 Game 162 win over the Red Sox, a game played at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida.
Bregman didn’t waste any time Sunday, either. Pete Crow-Armstrong led off the game with a single and then departed for pinch-runner Tyrone Taylor.
That was great to see. Bregman seemed totally locked in from the moment he stepped into the batter’s box. And that ball was crushed! [VIDEO].
Shōta Imanaga started for the Cubs and threw just the first inning, allowing a home run to Adley Rutschman. That was the 35th homer off Imanaga this year, second-most in MLB this year to Aaron Nola’s 37. Imanaga threw only 12 pitches in this game, which theoretically leaves him available to pitch in the Wild Card Series, maybe Thursday or perhaps even Wednesday. Apart from the homer, Imanaga struck out the other three hitters he faced.
Braxton Garrett, who the Cubs acquired from the Marlins at the trade deadline for minor leaguers Jonathon Long and Jace Beck and who’d been at Triple-A Iowa since, was recalled for this game and went into the game as the “bulk guy” and threw very well. Garrett threw five innings and allowed four hits and a run, though he did issue three walks. He threw 70 pitches and will be in the mix for a starting rotation spot next year.
Bregman drove in all four Cubs runs in this game and finishes with 93 RBI on the season. It’s so good to see him productive after that freak injury. Even if he is limited to DH duty for the Wild Card Series, as noted on the Marquee broadcast, he’s been the Cubs’ second-best hitter (behind PCA) all year and they are going to need that hitting. I noticed that Bregman was wearing a double-flap helmet on the basepaths, though as you can see, not when he hit the home runs.
BCB’s JohnW53 has this fact about Bregman’s two-homer afternoon:
Today’s game was Alex Bregman’s fifth of the season with multiple home runs. Pete Crow-Armstrong has seven such games; Dansby Swanson, three; and Michael Conforto, one, for a total of 16.
The Cubs had a team-record 20 such games last year. They had 19 in 2019, 18 in 1998 and 2004, and 17 in 1930 and 1958. They also had 16 in 2021.
Going into today, the Astros had 16 this year, second to the Rockies’ 18. The Padres had 15.
The Cubs flashed some glove while Garrett was in the game. Here’s a nice stop by Matt Shaw in the fifth [VIDEO].
Jacob Webb succeeded Garrett in the seventh inning and retired all three hitters he faced on just 10 pitches. I don’t think I have to tell you how important it would be if Webb could recover the form that got him 24 straight scoreless appearances before the big meltdown he had at the end of August in Seattle and Arizona.
Colin Rea entered to throw the eighth inning and also retired the Red Sox in order, on just six pitches.
The Cubs then put the game away with a three-run ninth. Miguel Amaya led off with a single and went to third on a single by Taylor. That brought up Bregman, and he came through yet again with this RBI double [VIDEO].
Fact about Bregman’s game from John:
Bregman is just the sixth Cub to hit multiple homers and also have at least one double, one single and one walk. He is the first to do so on the road.
Pete Crow-Armstrong did it in on Aug. 17 in the Cubs’ 10-inning, 7-5 win at home over the White Sox, with his second homer walking it off.
The four others:
Hank Sauer: May 2, 1954, in an 18-10, eight-inning loss to the Pirates
Ryne Sandberg: Aug. 10, 1989, in a 16-13 loss to the Phillies
Corey Patterson: Sept. 7, 2004, in a 7-6, 12-inning loss to the Expos
Chris Coghlan: Sept. 20, 2014, in an 8-7 win over the Dodgers
All had two homers, one double, one single and one walk.
Taylor stopped at third on Bregman’s double, but he then scored on this sac fly by Gabriel Arias [VIDEO].
As mentioned on the Marquee broadcast, Arias is a very good bench player. He can play all infield positions and his bat plays well enough, a really useful guy to have around. That made it 5-2. Ian Happ then struck out, but Michael Conforto doubled, scoring Bregman to give the Cubs a four-run lead [VIDEO].
Rea remained in the game in the ninth to finish up, and he recorded his second save. Here’s the final out [VIDEO].
In other postseason-related news, the Phillies won Sunday and so they take the final wild card spot and will face the Braves in Atlanta in another Wild Card Series beginning Tuesday. The Rangers lost to the Twins, which clinched the A.L. West title for the Astros (who are leading the A’s late and likely will finish 81-81). Houston will host the White Sox in a Wild Card Series starting Tuesday.
One more game note from John:
The Cubs’ six runs made their final total 850, their fourth most in the Modern Era, which began in 1901. They scored 998 in 1930, 982 in 1929 and 855 in 2008. They played 156 games in the first two seasons and 161 in the last.
And for whatever it’s worth, the win gave the Cubs an 89-73 record to the Red Sox’ 87-75. That means that if, somehow, those two clubs meet in the World Series, the Cubs would have home field. The Cubs have the better record over four of the six American League postseason teams; only the Rays and Yankees are better.
So the Cubs will now head to San Diego to begin their own Wild Card Series against the Padres Tuesday evening. I’ll have lots to say about that over the next couple of days here, of course. Michael King has been announced as the Padres starter, but no Cubs starter has yet been named. It could be Matthew Boyd, who’d be going on normal rest, as he last pitched on Thursday against the Marlins at Wrigley Field.
Game time Tuesday is late, so get rested up! 9 p.m. CT, with the game on NBC Sports Network (cable) and streaming on Peacock.
Go Cubs!

item.content:encoded:
Ronald Acuña Jr. continues to be one of the hottest hitters in baseball this September, hitting .342 with an OPS approaching 1.100. That late-season run got even more impressive over the weekend, when he locked up a 20/20 season despite missing more than 50 games to injury — the third time in his career he's cleared 20 home runs in a season shortened by at least 50 missed games.
Acuña hasn't just been one of the best hitters in baseball this month; he's reminded everyone he's one of the sport's biggest draws whenever he's healthy. Which raises the obvious question: Will the Atlanta Braves sign their franchise slugger long-term?
There are a few layers to that. Acuña is in the final guaranteed year of an eight-year, $100 million extension, with two club options for 2027 and 2028 that the Braves will undoubtedly exercise. But according to multiple analysts, a long-term deal getting done before he reaches free agency is far from certain, given both his injury history and general manager Alex Anthopoulos's general reluctance to make massive long-term commitments.
That hesitation has precedent. Anthopoulos and the Braves have let franchise cornerstones like Freddie Freeman, Dansby Swanson and Max Fried all walk away in recent offseasons, betting he could find comparable production for less money elsewhere — and largely, that bet has paid off, even if the solutions haven't all come from the same place.
Matt Olson, acquired via trade, has effectively replaced Freeman's production at first base, and a wave of young, club-controlled arms developed within Atlanta's own system has kept the rotation competitive behind Chris Sale even as Fried starred elsewhere.
Shortstop is a bit different. Mauricio Dubón has helped the Braves finally find a viable shortstop, whch they had been looking for since Swanson's departure. But even he's more of a stopgap in 2026 than the long-term answer, with genuine farm system options like Tatie Southisene, John Gil and Alex Lodise all competing to be the shortstop of the future.
Say what you want about those moves, but collectively, they worked. Freeman, Fried and Swanson are all great, even star-caliber players. Freeman is a future Hall of Famer. Yet, Atlanta found a way to replace each of them anyway.
Acuña is a different animal entirely. He's not just a star; he's a superstar, a sparkplug, the conduit every other piece of this offense runs through. We've already seen how much the Braves struggle with outfield-by-committee whenever he or Michael Harris II has to miss time.
Compare that to shortstop, where prospects like Southisene, Gil and Lodise are all competing to be the long-term answer, or even the rotation, where the system has produced options — the outfield simply doesn't have that same kind of depth waiting in the wings anymore. That makes keeping Acuña in Atlanta feel less like a preference and more like a necessity.
Acuña has an MVP under his belt, which he won after an unprecedented 40/70 season. Sure, they've let an MVP walk before, Freeman, an replaced him with an All-Star in Olson. Good luck doing that again and with even better ballplayer like Acuña.
That's why Acuña could be an exception to Anthopoulos's usual approach, and why he'll ultimately open up the checkbook before Acuña reaches unrestricted free agency in 2029.
There's also the competitive angle to consider. If Anthopoulos were to let Acuña walk, which teams are aggressive enough spenders to actually land him? The Mets, Phillies and Dodgers top that list — and even with Anthopoulos's track record of letting players leave for greener pastures, it's hard to imagine him handing one of the game's most electric superstars to one of Atlanta's three most bitter rivals.
The Braves face plenty of tough contract questions, but this one might be the most straightforward. Time will tell, but I think Anthopoulos will ultimately make the right call.

item.content:encoded:
We’re down to the final days of the 2026 regular season with still quite a number of teams that have something to play for -- including a few who are fighting for their postseason lives.
Such is the case with the Astros and Rangers, who are tied atop the AL West (with Houston owning the tiebreaker); the team that loses the division will most likely miss the playoffs entirely. Elsewhere in the American League, the Guardians and White Sox are still battling for the division title, though the loser of that should slot into the third wild-card spot.
While all the divisions in the National League have been clinched already, the wild-card race, specifically in terms of seeding, is very much heating up, with the Phillies, Cubs and Padres entering play on Wednesday in a three-way tie.
Which clubs will get to keep playing into October? And which will watch their playoff aspirations come to an end?
Our expert panel has ranked every team based on a combination of what we’ve seen so far and what we already knew going into the 162-game marathon that is a full baseball season. We also asked ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle, Buster Olney and Jorge Castillo to weigh in with an observation for all 30 teams.
1. Milwaukee Brewers
Record: 99-59
Previous ranking: 1
With the season down to a handful of games, the Brewers have all but run out of time for Kyle Harrison to recover his first-half form. Harrison was 8-2 with a 3.01 ERA before the break; he’s 2-3 with a 7.80 ERA since. His strikeout rate has remained steady, even as his velocity and movement measures have become more volatile. Meanwhile, his walk rate has more than doubled, and his homers-allowed rate has nearly tripled. Suffice to say, this is not a great combination of trends. Milwaukee has tried to get Harrison back in stride by using him out of the bullpen, but he’s gotten hammered as a reliever. Brewers fans who dreamed of a big three rotation of Jacob Misiorowski, Harrison and Logan Henderson probably need to recalibrate their expectations at this point. -- Doolittle
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Record: 97-61
Previous ranking: 2
We’re nearing October baseball, and it’s as if the Dodgers are knocking off items on a to-do list. Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup? Check. Edwin Diaz finding his stuff, finally? Check. Will Smith back in the lineup? Check -- and he has an OPS of close to 1.000 this month. Mookie Betts back to being Mookie Betts? Check. Kyle Tucker digging out of his seasonlong slump? Check. L.A. is putting the pieces back together just in time as it begins its effort to become the first NL team to go back-to-back-to-back. -- Olney
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Record: 96-62
Previous ranking: 3
Tampa Bay began the season with the longest odds to win the AL East. On Tuesday, it clinched its first division title since 2021 with a win over the Yankees. The Rays will enter their first postseason since 2023 as the favorites to win the AL pennant behind a distinct home-field advantage at Tropicana Field, a strong pitching staff and a dynamic lineup centered around MVP candidate Junior Caminero, designated hitter Yandy Diaz and first baseman Jonathan Aranda. With a payroll that ranks 28th in the majors, the Rays seek to become the team with the lowest-ranked payroll to ever win the World Series. -- Castillo
4. Atlanta Braves
Record: 93-65
Previous ranking: 5
Atlanta would’ve preferred to get a first-round bye in the playoffs, of course, but the fact that the Brewers and Dodgers seemed to have locked down the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds allows the Braves to treat this last week of the regular season like the last week of spring training. They can plot out the best way to rest their key relievers, assess the progress of Robert Suarez and arrange at-bats for the position players to be primed for the postseason. Meanwhile, the teams the Braves are likely to face in the first round -- the Phillies, Cubs and Padres -- are all still pushing for berths and home-field advantage in the wild-card round. -- Olney
5. New York Yankees
Record: 91-67
Previous ranking: 4
Despite manager Aaron Boone saying on Tuesday that Aaron Judge isn’t expected to return from his calf strain in time for the wild-card round, Judge told ESPN the following day that he does in fact intend to be ready for Game 1. He suffered the injury last Wednesday and was placed on the injured list two days later. The Yankees were initially cryptic about the setback, declining to disclose the severity and Judge’s outlook.
Boone offered some clarity Tuesday when he called it a “moderate strain” and acknowledged that the club does not plan on having him to open the postseason. Judge received a PPP injection Monday. The Yankees hope that will spur recovery. Otherwise, New York faces an uphill challenge to survive in October without its three-time MVP at his best. -- Castillo
6. Chicago Cubs
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 6
No player has made more of a second-half leap than Alex Bregman, whose season has just gathered momentum almost daily since the last week of July. That momentum was stopped in its tracks when Bregman suffered facial fractures last weekend when struck by a foul ball. The good news is that the Cubs decided against placing Bregman on the IL, believing he might be ready for the playoffs after.
But even if that proves to be optimistic, Cubs fans can take solace in the presence of icy-cool rookie Pedro Ramirez. The Cubs didn’t drop off much when Dansby Swanson was injured, as Ramirez provided a league-average bat and glove work at both second and third base that has kept an elite Cubs defense on track. You want Bregman in there, for sure -- but Ramirez provides a heck of a Plan B. -- Doolittle
7. San Diego Padres
Record: 88-70
Previous ranking: 8
San Diego’s magic number for clinching a playoff spot is shrinking, allowing general manager A.J. Preller and skipper Craig Stammen the chance to line up their staff for the wild-card series, with options developing. Stammen indicated to reporters that unless Michael King is needed to clinch a playoff spot on the last day of the regular season, he will be held over to start Game 1 of the wild card, wherever that is -- so he wouldn’t necessarily be used Sunday in order to win home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs.
Additionally, the Padres are in a better position to rest their bullpen, the perceived strength of the team. Adrian Morejon ranks third among all relievers in innings. Rest might be overrated for Mason Miller: He has made 16 appearances on zero days’ rest, and in those games, he has allowed two hits and one earned run in 16⅔ innings, with two walks and 27 strikeouts. -- Olney
8. Philadelphia Phillies
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 7
The culture of Philadelphia’s starting pitchers, from Zack Wheeler to Cristopher Sanchez to Aaron Nola, is to pitch deep into games. Unlike so many starters in this generation, Wheeler takes the mound expecting to work into the late innings -- and the Phillies will need this sort of production from the rotation, given the team’s recent bullpen problems. Orion Kerkering, an important part of the relief corps, struggled so badly that he was sent to the minors last week. Jose Alvarado has pitched better down the stretch, and hard-throwing Alex MacFarlane has quickly ascended into an important role in his rookie season in the bullpen. But the Phillies’ rotation will carry the team’s October dreams. -- Olney
9. Boston Red Sox
Record: 85-73
Previous ranking: 9
The Red Sox rewarded Chad Tracy on Tuesday for leading the team’s historic turnaround by removing his interim tag and giving him a three-year contract to continue as manager. Now he’ll look to accomplish what his predecessor Alex Cora couldn’t last year: beating the Yankees on the road in the AL Wild Card Series.
Boston has cooled off since going 32-5 to put itself in playoff position and faces some injury uncertainty going into October. Ceddanne Rafaela returned Tuesday after missing 16 games with a quad injury, and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand last Thursday and is dealing with soreness. On the mound, the Red Sox could receive two significant reinforcements for the bullpen in Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck. Crochet, last season’s AL Cy Young runner-up, has been out with a shoulder injury since late April, while Houck hasn’t appeared in a game in 2026. -- Castillo
10. Cleveland Guardians
Record: 82-76
Previous ranking: 12
Cleveland is, once again, showing its knack for a strong finishing kick. Over the past decade, only the Dodgers have won more September games. For Guardians fans aching for their team’s first title since the Truman administration, October is a higher priority at this point.
Like the White Sox, the first order of business is to secure the AL Central title and the first-round bye likely to go with it. Given the neck-and-neck nature of Cleveland’s battle with Chicago, there likely isn’t going to be much time for manager Stephen Vogt to ease up on the pedal to finish the season. That would be nice to do when it comes to rookie ace Parker Messick, who will finish the season with at least 50 more innings than he has ever thrown in a season. Messick has shown no signs of fatigue, so it may not matter. -- Doolittle
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
Record: 84-74
Previous ranking: 10
Manager Torey Lovullo’s comments in a radio interview last week in which he acknowledged that the Diamondbacks “probably” -- his word -- need to reach the postseason to earn him a contract extension surprised many in the industry, as Lovullo has a strong and long-standing relationship with his boss, Mike Hazen. The Ketel Marte situation has been challenging for the organization, with the team’s highest-paid position player failing to show up to the park, and owner Ken Kendrick has a reputation for being mercurial and demanding. Lovullo’s contract runs out at season’s end, and he and the Diamondbacks agreed they would discuss his status then. -- Olney
12. Chicago White Sox
Record: 81-77
Previous ranking: 11
The White Sox have wobbled down the stretch, but they have not fallen down. It looks like they will join the playoff party, completing an incredible two-year turnaround that saw them go from setting the modern single-season loss record to playing in October.
Barring a face-plant over the last few days of the season, the question of whether the Sox can overtake Cleveland for the AL Central title is the biggest remaining question. It’s impactful, with a first-round bye likely on the line. A bye is a boon for any team, but among likely postseason entrants, it might loom largest for the White Sox. That’s just because of how manager Will Venable has had to stretch his pitching resources to the maximum just to get to this point. A wild-card skip would give his staff at least a little time to regroup before the ALDS begins. -- Doolittle
13. Pittsburgh Pirates
Record: 80-78
Previous ranking: 14
Why did Paul Skenes lapse into baseball’s pitching middle class rather than continue his march toward Cooperstown? There is no bigger task for the Pirates and Skenes this offseason than figuring this out. With one more start to go, he has already allowed more runs this season than he did in his first two seasons combined. To be sure, it’s not all on Skenes, whose expected ERA, 3.27 per Statcast, is unusually divergent from his actual ERA (3.91). Still, even a 3.27 ERA is a far cry from the level of effectiveness Skenes flashed before this season. Why? Finding the answer to that question could prove to be the biggest addition Pittsburgh makes this winter. -- Doolittle
14. Texas Rangers
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 16
With eyes on the disappointing Mariners and Yordan Alvarez’s Triple Crown watch, the Rangers quietly remained in contention in the historically dreadful AL West all summer. Following three straight losses, they now find themselves tied atop the division with Houston. Texas will host the Mets in a series finale Thursday before finishing the season with three games in Minnesota. The Rangers will need to finish with a better record than the Astros, who own the tiebreaker, to reach the postseason for the first time since winning the 2023 World Series. -- Castillo
15. Houston Astros
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 13
The Astros fired general manager Dana Brown last month and are under .500 with four games remaining ... but they still have a real chance to win the division. That’s the AL West in 2026. The Astros finish the regular season with a four-game series in West Sacramento against an A’s team that has an MLB-worst run differential. The bad news: The Astros head there tied atop the division. The good news: They hold the tiebreaker over Texas. In the background over the last few days of the season: Alvarez’s push to become the first player to win a Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2013. -- Castillo
16. Toronto Blue Jays
Record: 77-82
Previous ranking: 15
The Blue Jays did not replicate their 2025 magic in 2026, largely due to injuries and their offense falling off a cliff. They finished last season fourth in the majors with a 112 wRC+; this season, they’re tied for 24th with a 95 wRC+. The dropoff starts with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and George Springer. Guerrero has nine home runs -- and, inexplicably, just one at home -- with a .695 OPS in the first year of a 14-year, $500 million contract extension. Springer, who reversed a precipitous decline to hit 32 home runs with a .959 OPS last season, has 15 home runs with a .730 OPS in 124 games this year -- and he’s a free agent after this season. Whether Springer re-signs or not, a rebound in 2027 starts with Guerrero sparking an offense that is tied for last in home runs in 2026. -- Castillo
17. Miami Marlins
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 18
Here’s the good news about the Marlins’ 2026 season: They hung around all year, battling among the contenders and having some individual successes. Here’s what’s not-so-great about where they stand right now: It’s hard to identify the players who could lead a Miami breakout into full-scale contention with the best NL teams.
Otto Lopez had an excellent season, but he’ll turn 28 years old next week and his OPS is under .800. Griffin Conine is the one player on the team with an OPS over .800, and he’s 29. Sandy Alcantara reestablished himself as a rotation leader, but he’s 31. Eury Perez has flashes of dominance and is just 23, but he’s got an injury history and will finish this season with an ERA over 4.00. More depth and more talent is needed for the Marlins to take the next step. -- Olney
18. Baltimore Orioles
Record: 78-81
Previous ranking: 19
Another disappointing season in Baltimore has already prompted some changes in the front office, but not at the top. President of baseball operations Mike Elias is expected to return in 2027. One move his front office got right was signing Pete Alonso last winter. The first baseman, who has played in every game this season, hit his 40th home run of the season in Monday’s win over the Blue Jays. He clearly isn’t why the Orioles aren’t going to the postseason for the second straight year.
Baltimore’s young position player core has not lived up to the hype, while the pitching staff wasn’t good enough to shoulder the load. Elias & Co. already decided to move on from former No. 1 pick Adley Rutschman, an All-Star catcher previously considered a foundational player, at the trade deadline. More significant moves could come this offseason. -- Castillo
19. St. Louis Cardinals
Record: 77-81
Previous ranking: 17
This rebuilding season has been an unqualified success for the Cardinals. If not for a leaky bullpen, their soft wild-card contention might have been a lot more solid. While bullpens are sometimes the final piece of the contention puzzle for a building team, that’s not always the case. Some clubs develop a bullpen-building process that takes effect even as the rest of the roster remains a work in progress. The Pirates of recent vintage are a good example.
Thus, the project of putting together a contention-worthy bullpen is a crucial one for the Chaim Bloom-led front office. Bloom was part of a Rays front office that annually churned out elite, no-name bullpens. However, during the four years that Bloom led the Red Sox front office, Boston ranked 24th in bullpen ERA (4.48) and middle-of-the-pack in save percentage. Good first year, but there is more to prove in St. Louis. -- Doolittle
20. Detroit Tigers
Record: 74-85
Previous ranking: 20
The Tigers will probably finish fourth in the AL in run differential, perhaps third if they pass the Red Sox, and will easily pace the Central by that measure. When you consider that, along with Detroit’s freakishly bad record in one- and two-run games (now 21-51) and the relatively short list of players on expiring deals (Jack Flaherty and Gleyber Torres, along with the retiring Justin Verlander), the Tigers are an obvious and very strong bounce-back candidate for the 2027 season. That doesn’t mean that president of baseball operations Scott Harris and his staff don’t have their work cut out for them when it comes to evaluating this lackluster season. Still, for the Tigers’ disappointed fans, it’s important to keep in mind that their team will be proceeding from a relative position of strength. -- Doolittle
21. Washington Nationals
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 23
In so many ways, the 2026 season was a success for the Nationals, who exceeded expectations this year, flirting with contention in the first half and seeing the development of players like CJ Abrams and James Wood into offensive stars. But the team’s pitching collapsed in the second half -- Washington’s second-half ERA of 4.49 ranks 25th. The Nationals locked down Cade Cavalli to a multiyear deal last week at the end of what has been a breakout season, but it’s clear that president of baseball operations Paul Toboni’s greatest challenge is to develop the sort of pipeline of pitching that will allow them to compete with the big-market teams in the division. -- Olney
22. Seattle Mariners
Record: 74-84
Previous ranking: 24
A year after falling one win short of the franchise’s first World Series appearance, the Mariners’ season will end Sunday with a whimper. The 2026 campaign will be remembered as the most disappointing one in franchise history.
Cal Raleigh’s drop-off from 60 home runs and an MVP runner-up finish was baffling. Julio Rodriguez regressed and still hasn’t made the superstar jump widely expected of him. Josh Naylor was a below-average hitter in the first year of his five-year contract. The starting rotation was not as good as advertised. Changes are inevitable, likely starting with manager Dan Wilson. But the Mariners can’t fire all of their players. They’ll need their core to bounce back from down seasons in order to rebound in 2027. -- Castillo
23. New York Mets
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 21
No one will go into the 2027 season under more pressure than David Stearns, the Mets’ head of baseball operations, following their collapse down the stretch in 2025 and the poor 2026 season. So it makes sense that he worked to keep someone he has a working relationship with in the managerial role, Andy Green, who had his interim tag removed and was hired to a three-year deal Tuesday. Steve Cohen’s comments on an SNY broadcast about needing new voices within the organization got the attention of a lot of rival executives, who wondered if the impact of Pete Alonso’s encore performance at Citi Field and the “Fire Stearns” chants last week made an impression on the owner. Under the circumstances, hiring Green seems like the right move for Stearns, the smart move. -- Olney
24. Minnesota Twins
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 22
The arrival of prospects Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez has the Twins’ prospective 2027 position group in good shape even if veteran Josh Bell declines his mutual option and departs. The murkiest position is catcher, where Ryan Jeffers is likely headed for free agency, presumably after the Twins issue him a qualifying offer. The QO could limit Jeffers’ market, but probably not that much, as Jeffers looks like the best free agent catcher option out there. If he leaves, the Twins will need someone to pair with Caratini.
Long term, after drafting Vahn Lackey third in the most recent draft, the Twins seem in good shape with him, Eduardo Tait, Khadim Diaw and Carson Tinney all showing well in prospect rankings. Alas, none of that quartet is likely to be a 2027 solution. -- Doolittle
25. Cincinnati Reds
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 25
The ongoing maturation of Elly De La Cruz, as he edges toward his career prime, has provided ample reason to keep an eye on the Reds, even amid a last-place showing. Still, there have been enough trade rumors regarding the supremely talented shortstop to make you wonder just how long De La Cruz will be around.
Recent comments made by his agent, Scott Boras, don’t help. Boras suggested to reporters that a future foray into the open market made more sense for De La Cruz than a below-market extension. What does that mean for the Reds in the near term? For now, he has three more years of team control, so there’s no reason to be rash. Still, with this cloud starting to form over Great American Park, some sort of clarity about how the Reds plan to deal with their best player would be nice. -- Doolittle
26. Kansas City Royals
Record: 68-90
Previous ranking: 26
The Royals’ biggest offseason project will be to figure out their 2027 bullpen formula. That process begins with evaluating the relievers already on hand. Presumed closer Carlos Estevez had shoulder surgery -- bafflingly not until the second week of September -- and the Royals almost certainly won’t pick up their 2027 club option on him. Lucas Erceg looked lost before being shipped off to Omaha, but he performed well in Triple-A and his velocity upon his return to the majors has been at its highest level all year. Which Erceg is the real one? Is journeyman righty Nate Pearson a leverage option? Does Craig Kimbrel have anything left? The Royals will need relief help from outside the organization, but how much of it will depend on the outcome of these evaluations and others. -- Doolittle
27. San Francisco Giants
Record: 65-94
Previous ranking: 27
The general perception of San Francisco’s farm system is that it improved in 2026, and Bryce Eldridge established himself as a player the organization could build around. Beyond that, however, the Giants really haven’t progressed. They have a top-heavy payroll situation, with hundreds of millions owed to Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Matt Chapman. The questions about manager Tony Vitello making the jump from college to professional baseball weren’t quelled by his first season with the Giants -- and neither were the questions about the man who hired him, Buster Posey, who is still relatively new to his front office role. -- Olney
28. Athletics
Record: 63-95
Previous ranking: 28
The A’s are stumbling to the finish line having lost 95 games. All-Star catcher Shea Langeliers recently returned from knee surgery, but several other prominent players remain on the IL, including Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, Jacob Wilson, Brent Rooker, Luis Severino and Gage Jump. They’ll enter their season-ending series against the Astros with a negative-217 run differential -- the worst in the majors by 33 runs. With one season remaining before the A’s move to Las Vegas in 2028, they enter the winter in search of a general manager after David Forst’s departure in early August. Their offseason priorities are straightforward: Get healthy and improve a pitching staff that has a 5.43 ERA (29th) despite pitching half its games at the launchpad known as Sutter Health Park. -- Castillo
29. Los Angeles Angels
Record: 60-98
Previous ranking: 29
The Angels, despite 11 straight losing seasons, are the only franchise in the majors that has yet to post a 100-loss season. That could change this weekend in Seattle, where the Angels will need to win three of four games to avoid reaching the century mark. It’d be a fitting conclusion to Arte Moreno’s tenure as owner. Last month, Moreno agreed to sell controlling interest in the team to Stan Kroenke for a record valuation of $4 billion. Kroenke will take over a franchise that has not appeared in the postseason since 2014 and has not won a postseason game since 2009.
The first order of business this offseason will be hiring fired general manager Perry Minasian’s replacement. The team could also be in search of a manager to replace Kurt Suzuki, who is on a one-year contract. It is a transformative time in Anaheim. -- Castillo
30. Colorado Rockies
Record: 57-101
Previous ranking: 30
Colorado has compiled 100 losses for the fourth consecutive season; the last team to suffer 100-plus losses in five consecutive seasons were the Phillies, from 1938 to 1942. In Paul DePodesta’s first year of running Colorado’s baseball operations, there were some under-the-hood improvements: the biggest run differential improvement of all 30 teams in 2026, an improved farm system and some nice finds for the every-day lineup, like Jake McCarthy, TJ Rumfield and Connor Norby. There’s still a long way to go to competitive relevance for the Rockies, especially given the high bar required in the Dodgers’ NL West. -- Olney

Cubs RHP Kevin Gausman leaves start after injuring left shoulder
(Photo credit: Patrick Gorski)
Chicago Cubs right-hander Kevin Gausman exited his Wednesday start against the visiting Miami Marlins due to left shoulder injury sustained while making a diving tag in the sixth inning.
After the game, manager Craig Counsell told reporters that Gausman's non-throwing shoulder 'got extended weird, and it just grabbed on him a little bit.'
Gausman told reporters that he dislocated the same shoulder in high school.
'I hope I wake up and feel great tomorrow, but you never know,' said Gausman, 35, who added he would take something to 'get in front of it tonight.'
Gausman, whom the Cubs acquired from the Toronto Blue Jays last month, allowed a one-out, two-run home run to Kyle Stowers in the sixth to give the Marlins a 2-0 lead.
After Heriberto Hernandez walked, Miami's Griffin Conine hit a grounder to the right of second base. Shortstop Dansby Swanson fielded the ball and threw to first base too late to retire Conine. Hernandez tried for third, and Cubs first baseman Michael Busch fired to Gausman, who was scrambling to the bag. Gausman caught the ball at his feet and lunged to tag out Hernandez.
However, Gausman winced as he got up. Counsell replaced him with Javier Assad, who was warming up in the bullpen.
The Cubs, who need just one win or an Arizona Diamondbacks loss to clinch a National League wild-card spot, have been dealing with pitching injuries all season, with 10 pitchers making at least eight starts.
Gausman, who is 9-12 with a 4.51 ERA between the Blue Jays and Cubs in 32 starts this season, is 4-2 with a 4.83 ERA in nine starts for the Cubs.
--Field Level Media

CHICAGO (AP) — Kyle Stowers homered and the Miami Marlins prevented the Chicago Cubs from clinching a playoff berth for the second straight night with a 3-2 victory Wednesday.
Dansby Swanson drove in both runs for the Cubs, who needed a win or an Arizona loss to Colorado to secure an NL wild-card berth. The Diamondbacks beat the Rockies 5-3.
Joe Mack’s groundout brought home Augustin Ramirez with the go-ahead run in the seventh and the Marlins retired the next nine Chicago batters to win their second straight game after dropping three in San Diego.
Stowers hit his 21st homer, a two-run shot, off Kevin Gausman in the top of the sixth to break a scoreless tie. The Cubs evened things in the bottom of the inning when Swanson laced a broken-bat single into left field to bring home a pair of runs.
Cade Gibson (6-2), the second of four Miami relievers, struck out two in the seventh and Sandy Alcantara worked the ninth for his second save.
Reliever Ryan Rolison (9-2) took the loss.
Gausman struck out seven and allowed two runs, six hits and a walk in the first 5 2/3 innings. Miami’s Ryan Gusto allowed six hits and two walks while striking out five in 5 1/3 innings.
Chicago’s Pete Crow-Armstrong needed a stolen base to become the seventh player to join the 40-40 club but went 0 for 3 with a walk and remained at 45 home runs and 39 steals.
Up next
The Cubs have not named a starter for Thursday afternoon’s home finale. RHP Tyler Phillips (5-6, 3.45 ERA) is scheduled to start for the Marlins.
